Wide-field photography serves as a valuable method for monitoring air quality, yet it frequently requires a calibration process that can be both time-consuming and costly. Projection grouping serves as a robust strategy for object pose estimation, delivering high accuracy and a reduced computation burden by restricting the matching process to the region of interest (ROI) around an object in the image. Additionally, the 2D object detection component has been adapted to operate within a depth map rather than a color image. Experimental validation confirms the effectiveness of the proposed pipeline, with results also demonstrating the utility of the expansion to work with 2D object detectors incorporating the suggested transformation.

It has long been established that every tree can be planarized by splitting its vertices, a result that also applies to every bipartite graph (Bender et al., SOCG.2016). Current natural language model training relies primarily on human-annotated text, which likely limits both robustness and generalization because it excludes countless plausible but unspoken alternatives. To address this, we introduce DISCO (Dynamic Information Disclosure for Selective Disclosure of Information), an approach that enhances training by incorporating noise that teaches robustness and fake notes that facilitate learning generalizations through the textual information they contain. Specifically, these synthetic data points are produced by modifying original human responses with noise and then modeled using a large language system. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by running experiments on two tasks: natural estimation of the true class of a text (e.g., sentiment analysis) and the more complex textual categorization tasks such as the paraphrase identification task: our findings reveal a significant improvement in the robust and generalization capabilities of the systems when compared to baseline models trained only on human-generated text. We provide further analysis on how the synthetic data modifies the semantic space and the theoretical underpinnings of the method in action.

We introduce the notion of a weakly natural transformation with values in categorical structures, using adjunctions as a key illustration. A weakly natural adjunction views the functorial mapping between two categories as part of a functorial adjunction between their composite monadic functors relative to the functorial functor from $\N$. This induced adjacency establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the initiality of an adjunction and the fact that it is universal, thereby offering a non-trivial, explicit, and unified framework for such adjunctions and the interplay between initiality, the exponential object, and the universal arrow.

The original Magnetospheric Absence model (MAD), developed by Domcke and Aharonovif 1983, successfully explained several MeV gamma-ray observations from Earth using hadronic emission frameworks. However, the model struggled to align with GeV data from the Fermi/LAT telescope. This discrepancy stemmed from the need for an artificially elevated electron heating rate in the magnetosphere to suppress synchrotron radiation; paradoxically, this same heating was required to amplify target density and enhance hadronic interactions to match existing data. We demonstrate that these MeV-range constraints also rule out synthetic scenarios that successfully reconcile GeV anomalies. Furthermore, we show the original MeV calibrations are incompatible with recent Fermi/LAT 12-year solar flares (SF17a and SF17b) analyses. Regarding more recent solar flares (SF17a and SF17b), our four-panel maximum model achieves compatibility with MeV data while explaining various aspects of the events that were unclear in the raw MeV data. Using a simplified electron population and advanced modeling, we explain the MeV data without excessive electron heating and successfully explain the SF17a and SF17b events while capturing features not previously explained in the MeV data using the MAD model.

This research introduces Advanced Echo Classification via Deep Contrastive Networks (AEC-DCN), designed for the automatic identification of cardiac disorders in echo datasets regardless of data scarcity or acoustic interference. The proposed approach functions as an end-to-end system that learns an acoustic image representation and recognizes specific echo classifications. The method employs a deep contrastive network to map acoustic images into a latent feature space, ensuring that points representing the same pathology lie close together while distinct normal and abnormal patterns remain far apart. A fully supervised classification head directly analyzes these latent features using the Mean Vector and Mahalanobis Distance (MVMMD) to handle potential head noise. Additionally, the model incorporates the Mutual Information and MVMMD (MI-MVMMD) variant without requiring supervised input at the image level for pathological identification. Comprehensive in vivo experiments on a dataset of 1800 echoes from 300 participants—consisting of three classes (normal plus two distinct shock waves)—show that the proposed model not only identifies cardiac disorders with high accuracy and efficiency but also pinpoints specific abnormal regions within echoes via the mutual information approach, demonstrating significant potential for automatic echo classification, "faulty region" localization, and clinical auxiliary diagnosis.

When $N$ is large (finite), the particle's velocity scales linearly with $N$, whereas in the thermodynamic limit ($N\rightarrow\infty$), the scaling follows $\sqrt{N}$. Parameter estimation for differential model data is commonly addressed via statistical likelihood methods combined with numerical solutions for the model's differential equations; however, these equations often possess no analytical solutions. In this work, we introduce a novel methodology that utilizes biological feasibility as a filtering mechanism to filter the solution sets generated by numerical solvers, thereby facilitating epidemiological data fitting for these models. We demonstrate the approach's utility by fitting the SIR model data to confirmed infection records from Peru during the initial phase of the COVID-19 outbreak.

A quantum system involving interacting atoms, where the conversion to molecules is suppressed due to a short characteristic collapse time, is analyzed using an effective non-rigid pendulum model. This approach captures both the qualitative behavior and certain quantitative aspects of collapse and collapse-induced phase transitions. Crucially, this pendulum framework clarifies interaction-driven collapse by highlighting the competition between a restoring force and a tangential explosive force; the resulting trajectory is governed by the ratio of the characteristic oscillation period to the collapse time.

We introduce a technique for identifying all viable partitions that include necessary delimiters. This approach starts by constructing a graph where each edge represents a valid primer pair; the partitioned data correspond to paths within this structure. Automatic High Dynamic Range (HDR) acquisition relies on a set of images taken with varying exposure levels, where the exposure algorithm plays a critical role in HDR quality. Consequently, numerous automatic methods have been developed to determine the necessary exposure duration for each image individually. These approaches typically employ deep learning models to estimate the optimal exposure, though the required training datasets must include image lists containing diverse and known exposure, saturation, and brightness metadata. This specific requirement poses a significant challenge for automatic data collection. This study proposes a method for the one-shot self-supervised learning of a camera's exposure policy. The proposed approach is adaptable, functioning effectively regardless of the specific deep learning model selected or whether the model was pre-trained. It also functions independently of the camera's internal exposure algorithms and does not need massive information about the specific device's characteristics, as the model learns the configuration directly. The proposed solution has successfully and accurately trained individualized models for five distinct cameras in a self-supervised manner.

Specifically, we address the variance in gate outcomes—such as those arising with emerging business trends—and present a computational approach for diagram nodes (representing activities) to activity similarities based on shared process contexts. Our method orders activities by temporal position within processes and employs graph similarity to identify diagrams sharing comparable workflows. Ultimately, we integrate activity semantic labels to evaluate Gradual Novelity sequentially through the process. We validate our model on a dataset of approximately 250,000 Wikipedia-derived articles and analyze a dataset comprising 170 distinct business processes.

This work introduces a constructive method for generating a finite-dimensional approximation of the Koopman operator applicable to a broad range of nonlinear systems. Our approach assumes the existence of a complete, finite set of generator vector fields on the observation space that map a specific function collection—spanning which the Koopman operator acts faithfully—closed under external differentiation. Concretely, we demonstrate the framework using polynomial observables for systems with cubic degree and trigonometric observables of finite order for a specific class known as $\delta$-persistent systems. Ultimately, this "Koopman generator" provides a unified generalization to existing techniques, streamlining the application process across diverse dynamical models.

We present SparseGAN, a method for neural generation of textual data from multiple semantic perspectives. The approach enables a set of semantically distinct views to compete for encoding a specific input sentence, resulting in a representation that is these features both sparse and efficient. This mechanism is implemented by training multiple generative adversarial networks, where each network is responsible for capturing a unique viewpoint. These networks collaborate via a generator composed of a sparse gating network, which integrates the individual viewpoints to produce a compressed and robust encoding of the source sentence. Due to the use of the sparse ALPAX format for generator parameters, the model adapts automatically to utilize only the most pertinent features from each perspective based on a given text, without requiring manual specification. We demonstrate via a cloze test that this method effectively masters generation from specific semantic angles and achieve state-of-the-art performance in standard benchmark evaluations.

We introduce a new, decentralized framework for collaborating on spatial capture-recapture (SCR) studies, known as the SCR-Cloud model. Traditional SCR data typically involve multiple individuals trapping animals within a defined area, where spatial encounter histories aid in estimating population density. Although standard SCR models thrive in localized, single-trapper settings, this author extends the model to encompass distributed traps across a larger, shared region. The proposed multi-trapper model draws analogies from Poisson binomial and multivariate Bayesian convolution neural network literature, offering density estimates that integrate information from all participants while preserving individual privacy. Two distinct algorithms process the combined dataset: an efficient binomial-based method provides maximum likelihood estimates, and a neural network facilitates both estimation and density simulation. The model's performance, including accuracy and coverage, is rigorously tested via simulation against conventional SCR and capture-recapture techniques. By the end of this research, statisticians and researchers will be able to estimate density over expansive territories by pooling data from many independent, small-scale sources.

The analysis of dynamical systems on multilayer networks is frequently hindered by the complexity of both theory and computation, particularly when examining the linear stability of non-linear states. We introduce a method that approximates the dynamics of $L$ interconnected layers by an equivalent system of completely decoupled layers. This model preserves the original inter-layer coupling topology and yields a simplified framework suitable for both theoretical investigation and computational analysis. Crucially, the approach maintains the linear stability characteristics of the non-linear states of the original multi-layer system. We assume both intra-layer and inter-layer interactions are defined by adjacency matrices, with the latter representing the reduction of inter-layer connectivity to vectorial dynamics among nodes. Under specific conditions regarding these matrices, the equivalent model proves effective across various dynamic patterns, including Synchrony, Taylor-Couette flow states, and activity-based dynamics.

The method employs a new class of estimators based on the proportions of specific transmitted packet patterns—comprising both full and partially filled packets—to calculate estimates for queue size. These calculations utilize the dimensions of the affected packets alongside the lengths of the corresponding intervals. The proposed nonparametric approach necessitates no prior assumptions regarding the stochastic nature of network parameters, such as data arrival rates or upstream transmission speeds. Instead, it assumes only that these parameters are deterministic or vary slowly relative to the rate of network filling. Additionally, the paper evaluates the proposed nonparametric strategies against parametric approaches in terms of both empirical performance and theoretical accuracy.

This study investigates the application of an optimization algorithm to identify and assess damage in self-sensing composite materials. Research focuses on self-healing piezocomposites, which contain polymer microcapsules embedded within an electroactive composite layer. Mechanical cracking releases a conductive black paint that alters the layer's impedance; simultaneously, impedance variations reflect strain field modifications caused by delamination or cracks in the main structural laminate. This approach has proven effective in detecting, localizing, and characterizing not only mechanical damage but also microcapsule rupture events itself.

Dynamic graphs offer a flexible framework for modeling temporal dependencies among diverse and varying entities; however, the approaches derived from them often fall short because static graph neural networks (GNNs) inherently struggle to capture both node dynamics and evolving interaction patterns. We introduce DECENNT, a novel embedded representation approach specifically designed for dynamic networks that unites coarsened self-attention mechanisms with exact message-passing techniques to capture various graph dynamics. By integrating precise neighbor information as a component of DECENNT, we enable it to function effectively alongside both static and time-varying graphs. Extensive testing across multiple tasks, including dynamic point-of-sale (DPOS) prediction and point-of-entity recommendation (PO2PO), demonstrates that our model consistently achieves superior performance compared current state-of-the-art methods.

Surveillance systems have historically proven valuable for tracking biological organisms within various domains, yet they frequently suffer from high false alarms caused by non-biological items moving in the scene. This study introduces a system architecture that merges flow-based detection methods with object-based techniques to isolate the trajectories of biological beings. By concentrating on the detection of people and vehicles, we demonstrate this approach, with results showing that proposed methods yield substantially cleaner outcomes compared to standard state-of-the-art flows and objects models, which are often obscured by background noise. While the specific examples focus on certain targets, the underlying principles are transferable to other scenarios and specific objects. These findings offer practical applications for the broader community, particularly in reducing operational costs and enhancing the functionality of existing systems.

Convergence constraints associated with pure Neumann updates often limit the effectiveness of domain decomposition methods. The Inception Domain Decomposition (IDD) algorithm addresses the nonlinear domain decomposition problem in the infinite domain by utilizing a domain dilation strategy. This approach establishes convergence rates dictated by the "inception depth"—defined as the minimum required iterations for a decomposition domain to completely encompass the support of the initial function. By strategically minimizing this depth, one can significantly accelerate convergence. Furthermore, the algorithm extends effectively to the finite case (finite iterations), where it prioritizes local updates near the boundary and gradually reduces the expansion distance. This not only narrows the overlap requirements between adjacent subdomains but also minimizes the volume subjected to computationally expensive nonlinear operations. The proposed method is applicable to various fixed-point formulations, including Crandall-Liggett and proximal algorithms, and has been implemented to solve the total variation flow and the nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

Underscoring the topological character of Anderson insulators presents a significant challenge within various physical setups. We introduce an efficient method for identifying these traits by establishing a one-to-one mapping between the spatial arrangement of on-site electron densities and both the Stief-Beerman (SB) and Chern numbers. Specifically, by examining the local symmetry in how an electron's density varies across lattice sites, symmetry-breaking patterns, or lower-dimensional lattice structures like chains, one can directly infer that the corresponding SB or Chern numbers are non-zero. As practical demonstrations of this framework, we consider the random-flux Anderson model, Anderson models incorporating symmetry-breaking defects, and, significantly, a three-dimensional Anderson insulator model. The proposed methodology is fundamentally geometric and offers intuitive insights, distinguishing itself from existing detection strategies such as Wilson loops, Levy points, or dispersive features.

Genus-one curve invariants were first introduced by Schaeffer, Stoll, and Sutherland with the aim of classifying these curves more effectively than generic generators. Currently, two computational approaches exist for determining these invariants: direct integration and utilization of geometric multiplications within the Jacobian variety of the curve. We examine the consistency between outputs generated by these distinct methods, a study motivated by our development of a new algorithm that implements integration by geometric multiplication. Our implementation features an adaptation of the weierstrass permutation. Extensive numerical tests were conducted comparing the performance of both multiplication strategies across various programming languages, ultimately facilitating the creation of a more refined integration-based calculator.

This study examines possible squark interactions with several classes of heavy Higgs bosons within the context of the Complex Supersymmetric Standard Model (CSSM). The experimental constraints and theoretical limitations imposed by the Stefanovik and Petrakis data are synthesized, focusing specifically on how squark masses ($m_{\tilde{q}}$) and their mixing parameters ($\delta$) are evaluated. The analysis highlights the distinct behavioral phases of these complex parameters and their varying impacts on the observed production rates of heavy Higgs bosons, specifically $A$, $H$, and $H^{\pm}$, relative to their dominant SUSY decay modes involving lighter squarks. Finally, a comprehensive summary details which specific CSSM parameter configurations satisfy both Stefanovik-Petrakis requirements and remaining boundary conditions.

This paper investigates the effectiveness of binary power control (BPC), a non-convex downlink transmission scheme, by comparing it against both optimal convex power control and simple random power control schemes. Theoretical findings confirm that BPC matches random control performance when evaluated per user rate, and both converge asymptotically to the optimal solution in networks with many users. However, because BPC's per-user rate limits scale quadratically with user count—unlike the quadratic scaling of total network rate—its efficiency remains constrained.

Although the fundamental rules governing how atoms interact remain largely unknown and complex, *ab initio* methods accurately predict microscopic properties based on atomic structures. Consequently, utilizing direct machine learning models to map local atomic environments onto physical outcomes has been a primary research focus for years. Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction as a powerful framework for understanding local atomic arrangements. To address this challenge, we introduce "DGL-JPEG," a novel, fully symmetric GNN designed specifically for atomic systems. Extensive tests demonstrate that DGL-JPEG consistently ranks among the most accurate atomic models identified in prior studies. However, because every tested GNN could theoretically learn perfectly symmetric representations, comparing these models is difficult when using standard loss functions that encourage such symmetry. Furthermore, achieving near-perfect symmetry extraction often results in significantly reduced predictive accuracy across various GNN designs. To resolve this ambiguity, we propose a new, partially symmetric intermediate stage in training. Our results indicate that adopting this two-step training strategy yields a distinct advantage: the model achieves a unique status that is both more symmetric *and* significantly more accurate than using traditional methods alone.

We investigate the impact of a capital city's infrastructural topology on the mechanisms of internal conflict. Traditional models typically simulate society as an all-to-all connected network, assuming uniform random interactions among individuals; in contrast, this study scrutinizes interaction patterns within realistic networks featuring non-uniform and topologically distinct characteristics. Our findings reveal that the topology of state infrastructure significantly influences both the initiation of civil disturbance and their subsequent evolution. Specifically, we identify two primary consequences: (i) disturbances require higher intensity to emerge in topologies characterized by high connectivity (high density) and (ii) the spatial distribution of resulting chaos varies distinctly across different topological designs. Civil disturbance acts as a characteristic state within our model, arising from an optimal spatial arrangement of non-conforming citizens. We posit these insights hold a universal applicability across diverse real-world scenarios, beyond the specific limitations of previous theoretical frameworks.

We introduce a novel knowledge distillation approach that enhances the training of an intermediate student by distilling from one or multiple larger teacher networks, grounded on a salience-based selection method for the subset of teachers used at each step. This algorithm prioritizes expert sources that best suit the current capabilities of the student, mirroring human learning strategies and facilitating more effective training than non-adaptive combinations, such as simple majority voting. This study demonstrates a 20% reduction in error for an ImageText classification student compared to the ensemble of image and text teachers, employing only two image and two text teachers as single-point examples. Expanding the dataset to additional image and text teachers yields only marginal improvements, with errors remaining roughly 20% higher than when employing just image and text teachers alone. The standard Lucas potential, $W_L$, effectively captures the non-equilibrium work relationship for an oscillating interface separating two phases within a system at out-of-equilibrium states. However, the curvature of the interface significantly influences $W_L$ through a now-unrecognized positive curvature correction term. This term correlates directly with the entropy change as temperature varies and can induce a reversal in the path of interface oscillation or even a complete stop in oscillation, both phenomena manifesting as hysteresis. These outcomes emerge even for sinusoidal boundary conditions that do not typically generate hysteresis in planar interfaces, directly attributing the effect to curvature. Since this curvature term is always positive, it stabilizes the disordered phase against the ordering phase, thereby suppressing hysteresis associated with the transition. By extending these findings to more intricate geometries and driving conditions, we offer a unified perspective on various observed hysteresis behaviors and predict new phenomena for experimentation to validate.

In population genetics, researchers typically model the ancestry of an individual as a density over combinations of source populations. These estimations often employ nonparametric techniques, such as placing prior distributions on the underlying admixture sources. While previous studies confirmed that a Dirichlet process (DP) prior on point processes successfully recovers a correct number of sources and their characteristic profiles, this approach frequently yields an incorrect distribution of admixture coefficients. The issue stems from the DP's constraint that the point process must be defined on a finite measure space. Consequently, the resulting model effectively normalizes the densities over a finite measure space, which typically does not align with the theoretically infinite Lebesgue measure. Node features in graphs can be effectively modeled using topological embeddings within geometric spaces, yet node feature representation within hyperbolic areas remains an unresolved challenge. We introduce the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), a novel approach designed to effectively encode various graph structures by mapping nodes into hyperbolic factoid spaces. LGCN distinguishes itself from current methods by formulating the graph convolution operation intrinsically within the hyperbolic environment, while simultaneously employing a Euclidean-based neural network architecture for the actual training process. To address common practical implementations of graph convolutions that rely on node features, we propose a specific type of distance matrix that directly maps the relationship between two nodes based on their spatial separation. This paper presents a conceptual demonstration of negative temperature using a two-level level system. By plotting inverse temperature ($1/T$) against energy within the possible states of the system, the distinct regimes of positive and negative temperature are clearly distinguished. We leverage this model to clarify several key concepts, including how positive temperatures yield negative results when combined with negative temperatures, and the mathematical rule for adding temperatures of differing signs. A complete set of formulas is provided to represent various physical phenomena under these negative temperature conditions.

We examine a minimal dark sector consisting of a single complex scalar field, structured around a "dark seesaw" mechanism that links the dark sector to the visible sector through a large mass splitting and dark parity symmetry. We find that preserving this dark seesaw mechanism is challenging due to potential instabilities in the vacuum state and subtle inconsistencies within the dark parity symmetry itself. To address these challenges, we propose a revised model featuring an additional, markedly lighter scalar field. In this enhanced framework, dark parity symmetry emerges robustly, and potential well analyses confirm high stability. Furthermore, our analysis of the Higgs self-coupling evolves from this lighter mass configuration, and we detail the implications of recent measurements of Higgs self-coupling from particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) within this specific model context.

Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) together with strong interactions and energy level splitting due to crystal fields defines the core physics of many transition metal oxides. This work introduces a general formalism and computational approach centered on an interaction term scaled by SOC to capture the formation of Mott insulating states where excited $d$-orbital levels are split by crystal fields but remain relatively weak in interaction strength. Initially, the model is validated on a half-filled $d^N$ shell coexisting with large SOC and significant crystal field splitting, demonstrating that the resulting band structure and single-particle spectra from numerical simulations align with those from a scaled effective model characterized by enhanced SOC and simplified, smaller interactions. Furthermore, the paper extends this scaled effective model to explore the nuanced balance between SOC and interactions in multiple archetypal compounds: La$_2$NiO$_4$, NiO, La$_2$CuO$_4$, and the tetrachloride of Ni. These systems involve either very strong or moderate SOC and cover a spectrum of crystal field separations and relative orbital energies. Consequently, the authors present and discuss generalized findings regarding the interplay between SOC and crystal fields as applied to both Ni- and Cu-based systems.

Detecting and forecasting disease outbreaks are of vital importance in public health, yet these tasks remain obstructed by the difficulty of accessing large, annotated image datasets. Addressing this, we propose utilizing generative models for disease mask-to-image synthesis, an approach that enables the augmentation of detection datasets by converting disease masks into realistic chest X-rays. To evaluate whether learned conditions for disease manifestation can be manipulated within the latent space to reflect specific clinical presentations, we contributed a newly created dataset known as Marmark, comprising 1,191 paired marked and unmarked X-ray images featuring five distinct pathological conditions: Atelectasis, Consolidation, Edema, Pneumonia, and Normal. Marmark marks the first dataset of its kind offering diverse disease masks paired with corresponding X-ray images for supervised geneic model training. Furthermore, we introduced four targeted latent condition manipulation algorithms designed to either inject specific diseases into "normal" images or modify existing disease types and severities. This collection of normal-looking but disease-augmented images with verified masks creates an ideal foundation for disease outbreak detection, particularly in scenarios where collecting self-supervised labels is challenging. The practical value of our proposed framework is showcased through two key applications: a superior performance in Pneumonia detection that surpasses baseline methods using real labeled data, and the successful simulation of four different disease states against five expected conditions in normal images.

达专家（ViDaExpert）是一个基于自然语言交互的智能数据可视化平台。该平台整合了大型语言模型（LLM）与生成式人工智能（GenAI）技术，提供了一个可扩展的组件库，包含由生成式模型自动生成的语义解析（SPA）及映射（GM）模板。ViDaExpert 能够识别用户 Prompt 中的实体并将其映射为对应的维表结构以支持分析任务；同时，利用多模态生成式 AI 能力，它可以渲染出相应的图表界面。此外，该系统还具备一个对话增强型模块，可用以补充维表等关键信息，从而实现即问即得的数据展示效果。这一功能不仅依赖于多模态大语言模型直接解析用户问题，还能通过调用基础 LLM 实现对初始答案的迭代优化，最终输出符合用户意图的可视化界面。
